dx: Testicular torsion with a bell-clapper deformity
case: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after he woke from sleep with sudden, severe pain in the left side of his scrotum. He has vomited twice. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. The left testis lies higher than the right, has a horizontal lie, and is exquisitely tender. The left cremasteric reflex is absent. Urinalysis is normal. Doppler ultrasonography shows absent blood flow to the left testis. At surgery, the left spermatic cord is twisted 720 degrees, and both testes are completely surrounded by the tunica vaginalis, which attaches high on the cord. Diagnosis: testicular torsion with a bilateral bell-clapper deformity. He undergoes detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy.

questions.stem: At surgery, the left testis is swollen and dark purple, and sections of a biopsy show interstitial hemorrhage with congested vessels. The cord is still twisted when the scrotum is opened. Which of the following best explains the hemorrhagic appearance of the testis?
options: Rupture of the tunica albuginea into the parenchyma
Venous outflow blocked while arterial inflow continues
Consumptive coagulopathy with severe thrombocytopenia
Reperfusion of necrotic tissue after spontaneous detorsion
approach: Picture what twisting does to the vessels in the cord: thin-walled veins collapse before thick-walled arteries.
Blood keeps entering through the arteries but cannot leave, so the testis becomes congested and bleeds into its tissue.
Rising pressure then stops arterial inflow, and the testis infarcts.
questions.why: Twisting of the spermatic cord compresses the pampiniform veins first because their walls are thin and their pressure is low. Arterial blood keeps flowing in for a time, so the testis swells, becomes congested, and bleeds into its interstitium. As pressure rises, arterial inflow also stops, and the result is a hemorrhagic infarct. This sequence is why salvage is best within about 6 hours of the onset of pain.
whyNot: Rupture of the tunica albuginea follows blunt trauma and causes a hematocele or intratesticular hematoma. This boy had no trauma.
Correct.
Consumptive coagulopathy causes widespread bleeding in many sites. It does not explain bleeding confined to one twisted testis.
Reperfusion injury can cause hemorrhage after a twisted testis untwists, but this cord was still twisted at surgery.

questions.stem: The bell-clapper deformity is an abnormally extensive investment of the testis by its serous covering. During development, this serous covering formed from which of the following structures?
options: Gubernaculum
Mesonephric duct
Transversalis fascia
Processus vaginalis
approach: Name the serous covering: the tunica vaginalis.
Trace its origin: an outpouching of peritoneum, the processus vaginalis, leads the testis through the inguinal canal into the scrotum.
After descent, the distal part stays as the tunica vaginalis, and the proximal part normally closes.
questions.why: As the testis descends, guided by the gubernaculum, a finger of peritoneum called the processus vaginalis pushes ahead of it through the inguinal canal. The part around the testis remains as the tunica vaginalis, a closed serous sac. In the bell-clapper deformity, this sac attaches high on the spermatic cord, so the testis hangs free inside it and can rotate. If the proximal processus vaginalis stays open, the result is an indirect inguinal hernia or a communicating hydrocele.
whyNot: The gubernaculum is a ligament that guides the testis into the scrotum. It becomes the scrotal ligament and does not form a serous sac.
The mesonephric duct forms the epididymis, ductus deferens, and seminal vesicle. It does not form the coverings of the testis.
Transversalis fascia forms the internal spermatic fascia, a fibrous layer of the spermatic cord, which is outside the serous sac.
Correct.

questions.stem: The surgeon notes that ischemic injury to the seminiferous tubules can release germ cell antigens and trigger antisperm antibodies. Which of the following best explains why the immune system treats these antigens as foreign?
options: Germ cell antigens first appear at puberty, after tolerance forms
Sertoli cell Fas ligand activates T cells that enter the seminiferous tubules
Leydig cell testosterone strongly stimulates lymphocyte proliferation
The blood-testis barrier forms in fetal life before T cells mature
approach: Recall when central tolerance develops: in the thymus, during fetal and early postnatal life.
Recall when spermatocytes and spermatids first appear: at puberty.
Antigens that appear after tolerance is set are seen as foreign, so the testis needs a barrier and local immunosuppression to protect them.
questions.why: Self-tolerance of T cells is established long before puberty. Meiotic and postmeiotic germ cells first appear at puberty and carry new antigens the immune system never learned to tolerate. The testis protects them with the blood-testis barrier (tight junctions between Sertoli cells) and with local immunosuppression. When ischemia, trauma, or surgery breaks this protection, the antigens reach immune cells and antisperm antibodies can form, which can reduce fertility.
whyNot: Correct.
Sertoli cells express Fas ligand, but it triggers apoptosis of activated T cells. It suppresses immune attack instead of promoting it.
Androgens tend to suppress immune responses. Testosterone does not explain why sperm antigens are treated as foreign.
The blood-testis barrier forms at puberty, when Sertoli cells mature and build tight junctions, not in fetal life.

questions.stem: The next week, a 19-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of right scrotal pain that has increased gradually over 2 days and burning on urination. The posterior right epididymis is swollen and tender, the cremasteric reflex is present, and Doppler ultrasonography shows increased blood flow to the epididymis. A Gram stain of urethral discharge shows many neutrophils and no organisms. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Escherichia coli
Mumps virus
Chlamydia trachomatis
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
approach: Separate epididymitis from torsion: gradual onset, preserved cremasteric reflex, and increased flow point to epididymitis.
In a sexually active man younger than about 35 years, epididymitis is usually caused by a sexually transmitted organism.
A urethral Gram stain with neutrophils but no gram-negative diplococci favors Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular organism that does not show on Gram stain.
questions.why: Acute epididymitis in young sexually active men is most often caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae spreading from the urethra. Chlamydia lives inside host cells and lacks a stainable peptidoglycan wall, so the Gram stain shows only neutrophils. Gonorrhea would usually show gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils. Chlamydia is often silent in men and women and also causes urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, reactive arthritis, and neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia. Nucleic acid amplification testing confirms it.
whyNot: Escherichia coli and other enteric gram-negative rods cause epididymitis in men older than about 35 years and in men with urinary obstruction or recent instrumentation. They would be seen on Gram stain.
Mumps causes orchitis, usually with parotitis, and affects the testis itself. It does not cause urethral discharge.
Correct.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause the same picture, but a urethral Gram stain usually shows gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils.

dx: Mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumor of the testis (embryonal carcinoma and choriocarcinoma) with gynecomastia
case: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a painless lump in his right testis for 2 months and tender enlargement of both breasts for 3 weeks. Physical examination shows a firm, nontender, 3-cm mass within the right testis that does not transilluminate, and 3 cm of tender, rubbery subareolar tissue in each breast. Serum beta-hCG is 48,000 mIU/mL (less than 5), alpha-fetoprotein is 4 ng/mL (less than 10), and lactate dehydrogenase is 410 U/L (100 to 250). Scrotal ultrasonography shows a heterogeneous solid mass with hemorrhagic areas. He undergoes right radical inguinal orchiectomy. Diagnosis: mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumor (embryonal carcinoma and choriocarcinoma) with gynecomastia.

questions.stem: Germ cell tumors of this kind, including those that arise outside the testis in the anterior mediastinum, occur with increased frequency in men with which of the following genetic disorders?
options: Fragile X syndrome
Kallmann syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome
Neurofibromatosis type 1
approach: Classify the tumor: embryonal carcinoma and choriocarcinoma are germ cell tumors, the group that makes up most testicular tumors.
Recall the main risk factors for germ cell tumors: cryptorchidism, prior germ cell tumor, family history, and Klinefelter syndrome.
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is linked especially to mediastinal germ cell tumors.
questions.why: About 95 percent of testicular tumors are germ cell tumors, which arise from germ cell neoplasia in situ and nearly always carry extra copies of 12p, often as an isochromosome. The main risk factors are cryptorchidism, a prior tumor in the other testis, family history, and Klinefelter syndrome. Men with Klinefelter syndrome have a markedly increased risk of germ cell tumors in the mediastinum. Testicular tumors classically present as a firm, painless mass that does not transilluminate.
whyNot: Fragile X syndrome causes intellectual disability and enlarged testes in adult men, but it does not raise the risk of germ cell tumors.
Kallmann syndrome causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia. It is not a recognized risk factor for germ cell tumors.
Correct.
Neurofibromatosis type 1 raises the risk of nerve sheath tumors, pheochromocytoma, and gliomas. It is not a recognized risk factor for germ cell tumors.

topics: Risk factors for testicular germ cell tumors

questions.stem: Sections from the hemorrhagic areas of the tumor are reviewed. Which of the following microscopic findings is most likely in these areas?
options: Syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblast with no villi
Uniform clear cells separated by septa containing lymphocytes
Glomerulus-like structures with a central blood vessel
Mature cartilage, squamous epithelium, and glands
approach: Link the very high beta-hCG and the hemorrhage to choriocarcinoma, the germ cell tumor made of trophoblast.
Recall its microscopic picture: malignant cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, with no chorionic villi.
Match the other patterns to seminoma, yolk sac tumor, and teratoma.
questions.why: Choriocarcinoma is made of malignant trophoblast. Syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG, which explains the very high serum level. The tumor invades vessels readily, so it is hemorrhagic and spreads early through the blood, often to the lungs. Unlike a hydatidiform mole, it has no villi. A normal AFP fits the absence of a yolk sac component, and embryonal carcinoma makes up the rest of this mixed tumor.
whyNot: Correct.
Uniform clear cells with lymphocytes in fibrous septa describe seminoma. Seminoma does not raise AFP and only occasionally raises hCG modestly.
Glomerulus-like Schiller-Duval bodies are typical of yolk sac tumor, which raises AFP. This patient's AFP is normal.
Tissues from more than one germ layer describe a teratoma, which does not secrete hCG.

topics: Germ cell tumor histology and markers

questions.stem: Serum estradiol is increased. Which of the following best explains this patient's gynecomastia?
options: hCG binding prolactin receptors on breast duct epithelium
Free hCG alpha subunit activating estrogen receptors
hCG inhibiting aromatase activity in adipose tissue
hCG stimulating LH receptors to raise estradiol synthesis
approach: Recall that hCG, LH, FSH, and TSH are glycoproteins that share an identical alpha subunit.
The beta subunit of hCG is very similar to the beta subunit of LH, so hCG activates the LH receptor.
LH receptor stimulation of Leydig cells and the testis increases aromatase activity and estradiol output, and the higher estrogen to androgen ratio enlarges breast tissue.
questions.why: hCG and LH share the same alpha subunit and have closely related beta subunits, so hCG binds and activates the LH receptor. High hCG from the tumor drives Leydig cells and surrounding testicular tissue to make more estradiol, partly by increasing aromatase activity. The rise in estrogen relative to androgen stimulates breast duct growth. For the same structural reason, very high hCG can also stimulate the TSH receptor.
whyNot: hCG does not act on prolactin receptors, which respond to prolactin and growth hormone, single-chain proteins unrelated to hCG.
The alpha subunit alone has no hormone activity and does not bind estrogen receptors, which are nuclear receptors for steroids.
Inhibiting aromatase would lower estradiol and would not cause gynecomastia.
Correct.

questions.stem: During the inguinal orchiectomy, the surgeon ligates the veins of the spermatic cord at the deep inguinal ring. In the cord, venous blood from the testis normally travels in a network that also cools the incoming arterial blood. Which of the following is this network?
options: Cremasteric veins
Pampiniform plexus
Prostatic venous plexus
Vertebral venous plexus
approach: List the spermatic cord contents: ductus deferens, testicular artery, pampiniform plexus, artery of the ductus, lymphatics, and nerves.
The pampiniform plexus wraps around the testicular artery and drains into the testicular vein.
This close contact allows countercurrent heat exchange, keeping the testis cooler than the body core.
questions.why: The pampiniform plexus is a network of veins that surrounds the testicular artery in the spermatic cord. Warm arterial blood gives up heat to the cooler venous blood returning from the scrotum, which keeps the testis a few degrees below core temperature for normal spermatogenesis. The plexus joins to form the testicular vein near the deep inguinal ring. Dilation of this plexus is a varicocele.
whyNot: Cremasteric veins drain the cremaster muscle and coverings of the cord. They do not drain the testis or wrap the testicular artery.
Correct.
The prostatic venous plexus surrounds the prostate and drains to the internal iliac veins. It is not in the spermatic cord.
The vertebral venous plexus lies around the spinal column and is a route for prostate cancer spread to bone. It is not in the spermatic cord.

dx: Ovarian adult granulosa cell tumor with postmenopausal bleeding
case: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician because of vaginal bleeding for 2 months. Her last menstrual period was at age 51 years, and she has never taken hormone therapy. Pelvic examination shows a firm, mobile, 9-cm right adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a solid right ovarian mass and an endometrial thickness of 14 mm (4 mm or less after menopause). Serum estradiol is 92 pg/mL (less than 30 after menopause), and serum inhibin B is markedly increased. Endometrial biopsy shows atypical endometrial hyperplasia. She undergoes total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Diagnosis: adult granulosa cell tumor of the right ovary with atypical endometrial hyperplasia.

questions.stem: Which of the following microscopic findings is most likely in the ovarian mass?
options: Papillae lined by columnar cells with psammoma bodies
Glomerulus-like structures with a central blood vessel
Eosinophilic cells containing rod-shaped Reinke crystals
Small rosettes of cells around pink material in a lumen
approach: Use the hormone clues: high estradiol and inhibin come from granulosa cells.
Recall the hallmark of granulosa cell tumor: Call-Exner bodies, small follicle-like rosettes of granulosa cells around eosinophilic secretions.
Match the other findings to serous carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, and Leydig cell tumor.
questions.why: Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors that copy the granulosa layer of a follicle. They make estradiol and inhibin, which explains the endometrial hyperplasia and bleeding in this woman. Under the microscope, the tumor cells have coffee-bean grooved nuclei and form Call-Exner bodies, small rosettes around pink fluid that resemble immature follicles. In girls, the same tumor can cause precocious puberty. A Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor causes virilization instead, and a fibroma can cause ascites and pleural effusion (Meigs syndrome).
whyNot: Papillae with psammoma bodies describe serous carcinoma, a surface epithelial tumor that does not usually secrete estrogen.
Glomerulus-like Schiller-Duval bodies describe yolk sac tumor, which occurs in young patients and secretes AFP.
Reinke crystals are found in Leydig cells and Leydig cell tumors, which secrete androgens.
Correct.

questions.stem: The tumor cells make large amounts of estradiol from androgen precursors. In a normal ovarian follicle, which of the following hormones induces the enzyme that granulosa cells use for this conversion?
options: LH
FSH
Prolactin
Inhibin B
approach: Name the enzyme: aromatase converts androstenedione and testosterone to estrogens.
Recall the two-cell model: theca cells make androgen under LH, and granulosa cells aromatize it under FSH.
So FSH is the hormone that induces granulosa cell aromatase.
questions.why: In the two-cell model, LH acts on theca cells to make androstenedione from cholesterol. Theca cells lack aromatase, so the androgen diffuses to granulosa cells, where FSH induces aromatase to convert it to estradiol. As the dominant follicle makes rising estradiol for about 2 days, the hypothalamus and pituitary switch from negative to positive feedback, producing the LH surge. Granulosa cell tumors express aromatase on their own, so they make estrogen without normal control.
whyNot: LH drives androgen production in theca cells. Granulosa cells gain LH receptors late in follicle growth, but FSH is the main inducer of their aromatase.
Correct.
Prolactin supports lactation and in excess suppresses GnRH. It does not induce aromatase in granulosa cells.
Inhibin B is made by granulosa cells and feeds back to lower FSH. It does not induce aromatase.

questions.stem: During the hysterectomy, the surgeon clamps the uterine arteries near the lateral cervix and takes care to protect a structure that passes just beneath them. In which ligament do the uterine arteries run, and which structure lies beneath them?
options: Round ligament, with the obturator nerve beneath
Suspensory ligament of the ovary, with the ureter beneath
Cardinal ligament, with the ureter beneath
Uterosacral ligament, with the internal iliac vein beneath
approach: Recall which ligament carries which vessels: the suspensory ligament carries the ovarian vessels, and the cardinal ligament carries the uterine vessels.
The uterine artery crosses over the ureter about 1 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix.
Clamping the uterine artery at this level puts the ureter at risk.
questions.why: The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament runs from the cervix and upper vagina to the pelvic sidewall and carries the uterine artery and vein. The ureter passes under the uterine artery close to the cervix, often taught as water under the bridge. This is a common site of ureteral injury during hysterectomy. The suspensory ligament carries the ovarian vessels, and the round ligament passes through the inguinal canal to the labium majus.
whyNot: The round ligament runs through the inguinal canal and carries only a small artery. It does not carry the uterine arteries.
The suspensory ligament carries the ovarian artery and vein. The ureter does lie near it at the pelvic brim, but the uterine arteries are not in this ligament.
Correct.
The uterosacral ligaments run from the cervix to the sacrum and help support the uterus. They do not carry the uterine arteries.

topics: Ligaments of the uterus and ovary

questions.stem: This patient's 66-year-old sister has a BMI of 37 kg/m2, normal ovaries on ultrasonography, and no hormone use. She also has endometrial hyperplasia. Which of the following is the main source of the estrogen that stimulates her endometrium?
options: Aromatization of adrenal androgen in fat
Direct estradiol secretion by the adrenal cortex
Estradiol secretion by ovarian granulosa cells
Hepatic synthesis of estriol from cholesterol
approach: After menopause, the ovaries have almost no follicles left, so granulosa cell estradiol is minimal.
The adrenal cortex keeps secreting androstenedione.
Aromatase in adipose tissue converts androstenedione to estrone, and more fat means more estrogen, which is unopposed because there is no progesterone.
questions.why: After menopause, most estrogen comes from peripheral aromatization of adrenal androstenedione to estrone, mainly in adipose tissue. Obesity increases this conversion. Without ovulation there is no progesterone, so the estrogen is unopposed and drives endometrial growth. Unopposed estrogen from obesity, anovulation, PCOS, estrogen-only therapy, or a granulosa cell tumor causes hyperplasia, and atypical hyperplasia is the precursor of endometrioid carcinoma. PTEN loss is the most common early molecular change.
whyNot: Correct.
The adrenal cortex secretes androgen precursors, not meaningful amounts of estradiol. Those precursors must be aromatized in peripheral tissue.
Granulosa cells are the main estrogen source before menopause. After menopause, follicles are depleted, and her ovaries show no tumor.
The liver does not make estriol from cholesterol. Large amounts of estriol are made only by the placenta in pregnancy.

dx: Ruptured corpus luteum cyst with hemoperitoneum
case: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of sudden right lower abdominal pain that began during intercourse 4 hours ago, followed by light-headedness. Her menstrual cycles are regular at 32 days, and her last menstrual period began 24 days ago. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 114/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 94/58 mm Hg. The lower abdomen is diffusely tender with guarding. Urine hCG is negative. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL (12 to 16). Ultrasonography shows a complex 4-cm right ovarian cyst and free fluid in the pelvis and hepatorenal recess. Laparoscopy shows 800 mL of blood in the peritoneal cavity from a ruptured right ovarian cyst. Diagnosis: ruptured hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst with hemoperitoneum.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of this type of cyst best explains why it caused serious bleeding?
options: Rich blood supply of the luteinized wall
Avascular granulosa lining of an unruptured follicle
Bilateral cysts stimulated by very high hCG levels
Implanted endometrial tissue that bleeds each cycle
approach: Place her in the cycle: day 25 of a 32-day cycle is the luteal phase, when the corpus luteum is present.
After ovulation, capillaries grow into the former granulosa layer as it becomes the corpus luteum.
A cyst in this very vascular wall can bleed into itself and then rupture into the peritoneum.
questions.why: After ovulation, blood vessels invade the collapsed follicle as it becomes the corpus luteum, which needs a rich blood supply to deliver cholesterol and export progesterone. A corpus luteum cyst forms when this structure fills with fluid or blood. Its vascular wall can bleed, and rupture, often during intercourse or exercise in the luteal phase, can cause hemoperitoneum and shock. Follicular cysts come from unruptured follicles, are less vascular, and may secrete estrogen. Theca lutein cysts are bilateral and follow high hCG.
whyNot: Correct.
This describes a follicular cyst. It arises before ovulation from a follicle that did not rupture, and its lining is avascular, so major bleeding is less likely.
Bilateral theca lutein cysts follow very high hCG in molar or multiple pregnancy. Her hCG test is negative, and the cyst is single.
Implanted endometrial tissue in the ovary forms an endometrioma, which usually causes chronic cyclic pain more than acute hemoperitoneum.

questions.stem: Sections of the cyst wall show an inner zone of large, pale cells with lipid droplets and an outer zone of smaller, darker cells. The large, pale cells developed from which of the following cell types?
options: Theca externa cells
Ovarian surface epithelium
Granulosa cells
Theca interna cells
approach: Identify the structure: a lipid-rich, layered wall after ovulation is a corpus luteum.
Recall its two cell types: large granulosa lutein cells inside and small theca lutein cells at the edge.
Granulosa lutein cells come from the granulosa layer of the ruptured follicle.
questions.why: After ovulation, the granulosa cells of the ruptured follicle enlarge, fill with lipid, and become granulosa lutein cells, which form most of the corpus luteum and make progesterone. Cells of the theca interna become the smaller, darker theca lutein cells at the periphery, which make androgens. The theca externa is a fibrous outer layer. Learning the follicle layers in order (oocyte, zona pellucida, granulosa, theca interna, theca externa) makes these derivations easy to predict.
whyNot: The theca externa is a fibrous connective tissue capsule. It does not become steroid-secreting lutein cells.
Ovarian surface epithelium covers the ovary and gives rise to surface epithelial tumors. It does not form the corpus luteum.
Correct.
Theca interna cells become theca lutein cells, the smaller, darker cells in the outer zone of the corpus luteum.

questions.stem: Her cycles have been regular at 32 days for several years. On which of the following cycle days did she most likely ovulate this month?
options: Day 14
Day 18
Day 22
Day 25
approach: Recall that the luteal phase is fixed at about 14 days because the corpus luteum has a set life span without hCG.
Differences in cycle length come from the follicular phase.
Subtract: 32 minus 14 gives ovulation on about day 18.
questions.why: The corpus luteum lives about 14 days unless hCG from a pregnancy rescues it, so the luteal (secretory) phase is fairly constant. The follicular (proliferative) phase is the part that varies, depending on how long it takes to recruit and grow a dominant follicle. In a 32-day cycle, ovulation is therefore about day 18. Menses begins when the corpus luteum regresses and progesterone falls.
whyNot: Day 14 is ovulation only in a 28-day cycle. Using it for every woman ignores the fixed length of the luteal phase.
Correct.
Ovulation on day 22 would leave a luteal phase of only 10 days, which is shorter than normal.
Day 25 is today. Her corpus luteum cyst could not have formed and ruptured if she had just ovulated.

questions.stem: At laparoscopy, the surgeon traces the ovarian vessels to the hilum of the right ovary through a short peritoneal fold that attaches the ovary to the posterior layer of the broad ligament. Which of the following is this fold?
options: Mesometrium
Mesosalpinx
Ovarian ligament
Mesovarium
approach: Recall the three parts of the broad ligament and what each attaches: mesometrium to the uterus, mesosalpinx to the uterine tube, mesovarium to the ovary.
The ovarian vessels reach the ovary through the mesovarium, after arriving in the suspensory ligament.
The ovarian ligament is a fibrous cord to the uterus and does not carry the main ovarian vessels.
questions.why: The broad ligament is a double fold of peritoneum with three parts. The mesovarium projects from its posterior layer and holds the ovary, carrying the ovarian vessels and nerves to the hilum. The mesosalpinx surrounds the uterine tube, and the mesometrium, the largest part, lies beside the uterus. Blood from a ruptured cyst collects first in the rectouterine pouch, the lowest recess of the peritoneal cavity when standing, and can spread up the paracolic gutters.
whyNot: The mesometrium is the largest part of the broad ligament and lies next to the body of the uterus. It does not attach the ovary.
The mesosalpinx encloses the uterine tube, above the ovary.
The ovarian ligament is a fibrous band linking the ovary to the uterus. It is not a peritoneal fold to the broad ligament and does not carry the ovarian vessels to the hilum.
Correct.

case: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a rash for 2 weeks, sore throat, and fatigue. Two months ago she had a painless sore on her labia that healed without treatment. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg. Examination shows nonpruritic, copper-colored macules on the trunk, palms, and soles; moist, flat, gray-white plaques on the labia majora and perineum; and painless, rubbery bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) is reactive at a titer of 1:64, and the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test is reactive. Diagnosis: secondary syphilis with condylomata lata.

questions.stem: If this patient is not treated, which of the following cardiovascular complications is she at greatest risk of developing many years from now?
options: Aneurysm of the infrarenal abdominal aorta
Aneurysm of the ascending aorta
Stenosis of the mitral valve
Vegetations on the tricuspid valve
approach: Recall the course of untreated syphilis: primary chancre, secondary rash and condylomata lata, latency, then tertiary disease years later.
Tertiary cardiovascular syphilis causes endarteritis of the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta.
Loss of blood supply weakens the aortic media, leading to dilation, aneurysm, and aortic regurgitation.
questions.why: In tertiary syphilis, Treponema pallidum causes obliterative endarteritis of the small vessels that feed the aortic wall (vasa vasorum). The ascending aorta and arch have many vasa vasorum, so their media is damaged most. The weakened wall dilates, producing an aneurysm, a wrinkled tree-bark intima, and aortic valve regurgitation. Other tertiary forms are gummas and neurosyphilis such as tabes dorsalis.
whyNot: Infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms are caused mainly by atherosclerosis, not by syphilis.
Correct.
Mitral stenosis is a late complication of rheumatic heart disease after group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
Tricuspid valve vegetations are typical of infective endocarditis in people who inject drugs.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a reactive VDRL test on routine screening. Her FTA-ABS is nonreactive, and she has no signs of syphilis. Which of the following best explains her VDRL result?
options: Antiphospholipid antibodies binding cardiolipin
Cross-reacting antibodies to treponemal surface proteins
Persistent antibodies from syphilis treated years earlier
Rheumatoid factor binding to Treponema pallidum antigens
approach: Sort the tests: VDRL and RPR are nontreponemal tests that detect antibodies to a cardiolipin, lecithin, and cholesterol antigen.
FTA-ABS is a treponemal test that detects antibodies to the organism itself.
A reactive nontreponemal test with a nonreactive treponemal test is a false positive, and SLE causes this through antiphospholipid antibodies.
questions.why: Nontreponemal tests use cardiolipin, a phospholipid, as their antigen. Patients with SLE and antiphospholipid antibodies, as well as pregnant women and people with some viral infections, can have antibodies that react with it, giving a false-positive VDRL or RPR. The treponemal FTA-ABS detects antibodies to T. pallidum itself, so it is nonreactive here. In real syphilis, nontreponemal titers rise with active disease and fall after treatment, while treponemal tests usually stay reactive for life.
whyNot: Correct.
Antibodies to treponemal proteins would make the FTA-ABS reactive. Her FTA-ABS is nonreactive.
Past treated syphilis usually leaves a reactive FTA-ABS for life. A nonreactive FTA-ABS argues against prior infection.
Rheumatoid factor is an antibody to the Fc region of IgG. It does not bind treponemal antigens or explain a cardiolipin-based result.

questions.stem: Her inguinal lymphadenopathy reflects drainage from the vulvar and perineal lesions. If her primary chancre had instead been on the cervix, to which of the following lymph node groups would infection most likely have spread first?
options: Superficial and deep inguinal nodes
Inferior mesenteric nodes
Internal and external iliac nodes
Para-aortic (lumbar) nodes
approach: Recall that the vulva, perineum, and distal vagina drain to the superficial inguinal nodes, which is why her groin nodes are enlarged.
The cervix and upper vagina drain laterally along the uterine vessels in the parametrium.
These lymphatics reach the internal and external iliac nodes, including the obturator nodes.
questions.why: Lymph drainage follows embryologic origin and blood supply. The cervix and upper vagina drain through the parametrium along the uterine vessels to the internal and external iliac nodes, and then to the common iliac nodes. The vulva and distal vagina drain to the superficial inguinal nodes. The ovaries drain with the ovarian vessels to the para-aortic nodes. This is why a cervical chancre often causes no palpable groin nodes.
whyNot: Inguinal nodes drain the vulva, perineum, distal vagina, and lower limb, which is why this patient's groin nodes are enlarged now. The cervix does not drain there first.
Inferior mesenteric nodes drain the distal colon and upper rectum, not the cervix.
Correct.
Para-aortic nodes drain the ovaries and testes, following the gonadal vessels.

questions.stem: Routine cervical cytology from this patient shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. HPV genotyping is performed. Which of the following HPV types is most likely to be found?
options: Types 1, 2, and 4
Types 5 and 8
Types 6 and 11
Types 16 and 18
approach: Recognize that a high-grade squamous lesion of the cervix is a precancer driven by high-risk HPV.
Separate low-risk types 6 and 11, which cause condylomata acuminata, from high-risk types such as 16 and 18.
Types 16 and 18 cause most cervical, vulvar, vaginal, penile, anal, and oropharyngeal squamous carcinomas.
questions.why: High-risk HPV types, chiefly 16 and 18, make E6 and E7 proteins that inactivate p53 and RB, which allows dysplasia and carcinoma to develop. They cause most high-grade cervical lesions and also carcinomas of the vulva, vagina, penis, anus, and oropharynx. Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause condylomata acuminata, which show koilocytes. Condylomata lata, like this patient's perineal plaques, are lesions of secondary syphilis full of spirochetes.
whyNot: Types 1, 2, and 4 cause common and plantar warts on the skin. They do not cause cervical dysplasia.
Types 5 and 8 are linked with skin cancers in epidermodysplasia verruciformis, not with cervical disease.
Types 6 and 11 are low-risk types that cause condylomata acuminata and low-grade lesions, not high-grade dysplasia.
Correct.

dx: Gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease with Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis
case: A 23-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of lower abdominal pain and purulent vaginal discharge for 3 days and right upper quadrant pain that is worse with deep breathing for 1 day. Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. The right upper quadrant is tender. Pelvic examination shows mucopurulent cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness, and bilateral adnexal tenderness. Urine hCG is negative. Leukocyte count is 15,200/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). Serum aminotransferases are within normal limits. Nucleic acid amplification testing of a cervical swab is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Diagnosis: gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease with Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis.

questions.stem: An endocervical culture on Thayer-Martin agar grows oxidase-positive, gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following additional results would distinguish this organism from Neisseria meningitidis?
options: Growth on Thayer-Martin agar
Positive oxidase reaction
Fermentation of glucose only
Diplococci with flat adjacent sides
approach: List what the two pathogenic Neisseria share: gram-negative kidney-bean diplococci, oxidase positive, and growth on Thayer-Martin agar.
Recall the sugar test: N. meningitidis ferments maltose and glucose, while N. gonorrhoeae ferments glucose only.
So glucose fermentation without maltose fermentation identifies N. gonorrhoeae.
questions.why: N. gonorrhoeae and N. meningitidis look alike on Gram stain, are both oxidase positive, and both grow on Thayer-Martin agar, a selective chocolate agar with antibiotics that suppress normal flora. The classic separating test is carbohydrate use: gonococci ferment only glucose, and meningococci ferment both glucose and maltose. Gonococci also lack a polysaccharide capsule, and they rely on pili with antigenic variation, IgA protease, and lipooligosaccharide for disease.
whyNot: Thayer-Martin agar supports both pathogenic Neisseria species. It separates them from normal flora, not from each other.
Both species are oxidase positive, so this result does not separate them.
Correct.
Both species appear as kidney-bean diplococci with flat adjacent sides.

questions.stem: This patient asks whether this infection could affect her ability to become pregnant later. Which of the following mechanisms causes most of the tubal damage that leads to infertility after salpingitis?
options: Direct lysis of the tubal muscularis by a pore-forming exotoxin
Caseating granulomas that replace the tubal mucosa
Antibody-mediated attack on tubal smooth muscle antigens
Host neutrophil and cytokine injury that heals by fibrosis
approach: Recall that gonococcal lipooligosaccharide and peptidoglycan trigger a strong innate immune response.
Neutrophils and cytokines such as TNF damage the ciliated tubal epithelium.
Healing by scarring causes adhesions and blockage, which leads to infertility and raises the risk of ectopic pregnancy, and the risk climbs with each episode.
questions.why: Most tubal damage in gonococcal and chlamydial salpingitis comes from the host's own inflammation. Bacterial products stimulate neutrophils and cytokines such as TNF, which kill ciliated cells and damage the mucosal folds. The tube heals by fibrosis, which can close it completely (infertility) or narrow it and slow the embryo (ectopic pregnancy). Repeated or untreated infections cause more scarring, so the risk rises with each episode.
whyNot: N. gonorrhoeae does not make a pore-forming exotoxin that lyses tubal muscle. Its damage comes mainly from inflammation triggered by lipooligosaccharide.
Caseating granulomas describe tuberculous salpingitis, an uncommon cause of tubal infertility in the United States.
Salpingitis is not a type II hypersensitivity reaction against tubal smooth muscle.
Correct.

questions.stem: She does not complete her antibiotic course. Twelve days later, she returns with a temperature of 39.1 °C (102.4 °F), worsening left pelvic pain, and a tender left adnexal fullness. Urine hCG is negative. Ultrasonography shows a 6-cm thick-walled, multilocular left adnexal mass with internal debris. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Tubo-ovarian abscess
Endometrioma
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Hydrosalpinx
approach: Note the setting: incompletely treated PID followed by high fever and a new complex adnexal mass.
Infection spreading from the tube to the ovary forms an inflammatory mass filled with pus.
A negative hCG rules out ectopic pregnancy, and the fever and debris argue against a sterile cyst.
questions.why: A tubo-ovarian abscess forms when salpingitis spreads to the ovary and the inflamed tube and ovary fuse into a walled-off collection of pus. It shows up as fever, pelvic pain, and a thick-walled, multilocular adnexal mass with debris. It can rupture and cause life-threatening peritonitis. Other complications of salpingitis include hydrosalpinx, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis.
whyNot: Correct.
An endometrioma is a chocolate cyst from ovarian endometriosis. It causes cyclic pain, not high fever after PID.
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy needs a positive hCG. Her hCG is negative.
A hydrosalpinx is a late, sterile, fluid-filled tube after the infection heals. It is thin-walled and does not cause high fever.

questions.stem: Fertilization normally takes place in the ampulla of the uterine tube, the region often damaged by salpingitis. When a sperm fuses with the ovulated oocyte in the ampulla, which of the following events occurs in the oocyte?
options: Completion of meiosis I, releasing the first polar body
Completion of meiosis II, releasing the second polar body
Exit from the diplotene stage of prophase I arrest
First mitotic cleavage while still inside the corona radiata
approach: Recall the two arrests: prophase I (diplotene) from fetal life until the LH surge, then metaphase II from ovulation until fertilization.
At ovulation, the oocyte is already a secondary oocyte held in metaphase II.
Sperm entry triggers a calcium wave that completes meiosis II and releases the second polar body.
questions.why: Primary oocytes stay arrested in prophase I from fetal life until the LH surge before ovulation, when they finish meiosis I and release the first polar body. The secondary oocyte then arrests in metaphase II. Sperm fusion in the ampulla raises calcium inside the oocyte, which completes meiosis II, releases the second polar body, and starts the cortical reaction that blocks other sperm. The male and female pronuclei then form and fuse.
whyNot: Meiosis I is completed before ovulation, in response to the LH surge, not at fertilization.
Correct.
Exit from the diplotene arrest happens with the LH surge, before ovulation.
The first cleavage happens about a day after fertilization, after the pronuclei fuse.

case: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, comes to the physician at 26 weeks' gestation for a follow-up visit. Her blood group is O, Rh(D) negative, and her partner is Rh(D) positive. Her first child, born 5 years ago, is Rh(D) positive and was healthy at birth, and she did not receive anti-D immune globulin after that delivery. Her anti-D antibody titer is 1:256 (critical titer about 1:16). Ultrasonography shows fetal ascites, pleural effusions, and scalp edema, and Doppler study shows an increased peak systolic velocity in the fetal middle cerebral artery, consistent with severe fetal anemia. Diagnosis: Rh alloimmunization with fetal hydrops. Intrauterine transfusion is planned.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her first child was not affected?
options: Her anti-D antibodies during that pregnancy were of the IgE class
Fetal red cells in a first pregnancy do not yet express the D antigen
Placental transport of IgG begins only in a second pregnancy
Fetal red cells reached her blood mainly at delivery
approach: Recall when fetal red cells enter the mother in large numbers: at delivery, when the placenta separates.
Her first exposure therefore came too late to harm the first baby, and the first response is mostly IgM, which cannot cross the placenta.
In the next Rh-positive pregnancy, memory B cells make high-affinity anti-D IgG, which crosses the placenta and causes type II hypersensitivity hemolysis.
questions.why: An Rh-negative woman usually meets Rh-positive fetal red cells in quantity at delivery, so the first baby is born before her immune response develops. Her primary response makes IgM and memory B cells. In a later Rh-positive pregnancy, even small fetomaternal bleeds trigger a fast IgG response. Anti-D IgG crosses the placenta, coats fetal red cells, and they are destroyed by macrophages in the fetal spleen, a type II hypersensitivity reaction. Severe anemia causes high-output heart failure and hydrops. Anti-D immune globulin after delivery prevents this sensitization.
whyNot: IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity and does not destroy red cells. The antibodies in Rh disease are IgM at first and then IgG.
The D antigen is present on fetal red cells early in gestation, in first and later pregnancies alike.
Placental FcRn transports IgG in every pregnancy. A first pregnancy is spared because the mother has not yet made anti-D IgG.
Correct.

questions.stem: For the intrauterine transfusion, a needle is guided into the umbilical vein near the placental cord insertion. Which of the following best describes this vessel?
options: A single vessel carrying oxygenated blood to the fetus
One of two vessels carrying oxygenated blood to the fetus
One of two vessels carrying deoxygenated blood to the placenta
A single vessel carrying deoxygenated blood to the placenta
approach: Recall the normal umbilical cord: two arteries and one vein in Wharton jelly.
Name vessels by the direction of flow relative to the fetal heart: arteries leave the fetus and veins return to it.
So the single umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus.
questions.why: The umbilical cord normally holds two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein, cushioned by Wharton jelly. The arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetal internal iliac arteries to the placenta, and the vein returns oxygenated blood to the fetus, much of it through the ductus venosus to the inferior vena cava. Red cells transfused into the vein therefore go straight into the fetal circulation. The placenta itself forms from fetal chorion frondosum and maternal decidua basalis.
whyNot: Correct.
There is only one umbilical vein in a normal cord. The right umbilical vein regresses early in development.
This describes the umbilical arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood away from the fetus to the placenta.
Deoxygenated blood leaves the fetus in the two umbilical arteries, not in a single vessel.

questions.stem: Before her procedure, an arterial blood gas analysis is obtained while she breathes room air and is comfortable. Reference ranges are pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 22 to 28 mEq/L. Which of the following sets of results is most likely in a healthy woman at this stage of pregnancy?
options: pH 7.32, PaCO2 50 mm Hg, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L
pH 7.40, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L
pH 7.44, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L
pH 7.48, PaCO2 41 mm Hg, bicarbonate 30 mEq/L
approach: Recall that progesterone stimulates the respiratory center, which increases tidal volume and minute ventilation.
More ventilation lowers PaCO2, producing a respiratory alkalosis.
The kidneys compensate by excreting bicarbonate, so pH stays near the upper end of normal.
questions.why: In pregnancy, progesterone raises the sensitivity of the respiratory center to carbon dioxide, so minute ventilation rises by about 30 to 50 percent, mainly through larger tidal volumes. PaCO2 falls to about 30 mm Hg, and the kidneys lower bicarbonate to about 20 mEq/L, giving a compensated respiratory alkalosis. The lower maternal PaCO2 also helps carbon dioxide move from fetus to mother. Other normal changes include higher plasma volume, cardiac output, and GFR, lower vascular resistance, and hypercoagulability.
whyNot: A low pH with a high PaCO2 is respiratory acidosis, the opposite of the hyperventilation of pregnancy.
These are nonpregnant normal values. They do not show the lower PaCO2 expected in pregnancy.
Correct.
A high pH with high bicarbonate and normal PaCO2 is metabolic alkalosis, as seen with vomiting, not a normal pregnancy.

questions.stem: Her antibodies destroy fetal red cells, yet trophoblast, which also carries paternal antigens, is not rejected. Extravillous trophoblast that invades the decidua lacks classical HLA-A and HLA-B, and loss of these molecules ordinarily marks a cell for killing by natural killer cells. Which of the following best explains why uterine natural killer cells do not kill these trophoblast cells?
options: High expression of HLA-A and HLA-B that inhibits NK cells
Expression of HLA-G that engages NK cell inhibitory receptors
Expression of HLA-DR that induces maternal regulatory T cells
Complete absence of HLA molecules that hides the cells from NK cells
approach: Recall the missing-self rule: NK cells kill cells that lack class I HLA unless an inhibitory receptor is engaged.
Extravillous trophoblast lacks HLA-A and HLA-B, which protects it from maternal T cells that would see paternal antigens.
It expresses the nonclassical class I molecule HLA-G instead, which binds inhibitory receptors on NK cells and stops them from killing.
questions.why: The fetus is semiallogeneic, so maternal T cells could recognize paternal HLA-A and HLA-B on trophoblast. Trophoblast avoids this by not expressing those classical molecules. Losing class I HLA would normally invite NK cell attack, but the extravillous trophoblast that meets uterine NK cells in the decidua expresses HLA-G, a nonclassical class I molecule with little variation, which binds inhibitory receptors on uterine NK cells. Fetal red cells are a separate target, because maternal IgG crosses the placenta and binds the D antigen directly.
whyNot: Extravillous trophoblast does not express HLA-A or HLA-B. If it did, maternal T cells could recognize paternal alleles.
Correct.
Trophoblast does not express class II molecules such as HLA-DR.
Extravillous trophoblast still expresses some class I molecules, including HLA-G. A cell with no HLA class I at all would be killed by NK cells under the missing-self rule, not hidden from them.

dx: Early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis in a newborn after prolonged rupture of membranes
case: A newborn girl is evaluated in the nursery 14 hours after birth because of grunting and poor feeding. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation to a 26-year-old woman whose membranes ruptured 22 hours before delivery. The mother's group B streptococcal status was unknown, her temperature during labor was 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), and she received no intrapartum antibiotics. The infant's temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 182/min, respirations are 72/min, and blood pressure is 50/28 mm Hg. Capillary refill is delayed. Blood culture grows beta-hemolytic, gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase negative, bacitracin resistant, and CAMP positive. Diagnosis: early-onset group B streptococcal (Streptococcus agalactiae) sepsis.

questions.stem: This infant acquired the infection from vaginal flora during labor. Which of the following organisms is most often transmitted to the fetus across the placenta instead?
options: Chlamydia trachomatis
Toxoplasma gondii
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Herpes simplex virus type 2
approach: Recall that group B streptococci colonize the vagina and rectum and reach the infant during labor, especially after prolonged rupture of membranes.
Sort the TORCH and genital organisms by route: across the placenta or during passage through the birth canal.
Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and Treponema pallidum cross the placenta, while chlamydia, gonorrhea, and most neonatal herpes are acquired at delivery.
questions.why: Streptococcus agalactiae is a beta-hemolytic, bacitracin-resistant, CAMP-positive organism that colonizes the vagina of many healthy women. It reaches the infant during labor and causes early-onset sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis. TORCH organisms, by contrast, are known for crossing the placenta. Toxoplasma gondii, acquired by the mother from cat feces or undercooked meat, crosses the placenta and can cause chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications.
whyNot: Chlamydia trachomatis is acquired during vaginal delivery and causes conjunctivitis and afebrile pneumonia in the first weeks of life.
Correct.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is acquired during delivery and causes purulent conjunctivitis within the first few days of life.
About 85 percent of neonatal herpes is acquired during delivery from maternal genital infection. Transplacental infection is rare.

questions.stem: The mother's labor was augmented with an intravenous oxytocin infusion. Which of the following intracellular events most directly mediated the stronger uterine contractions?
options: Gs-coupled rise in cyclic AMP in myometrial cells
Opening of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor channels
Gq-coupled release of intracellular calcium
Binding of oxytocin to nuclear hormone receptors
approach: Recall that the oxytocin receptor is a Gq-coupled receptor on myometrial cells.
Gq activates phospholipase C, which makes IP3 and releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Calcium binds calmodulin and activates myosin light-chain kinase, so the smooth muscle contracts. Oxytocin also increases prostaglandin production, adding to the effect.
questions.why: Oxytocin binds Gq-coupled receptors on myometrium, which multiply near term under estrogen. Phospholipase C makes IP3, which releases stored calcium, and calcium-calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase to drive contraction. Oxytocin also stimulates prostaglandin synthesis in the decidua, which strengthens contractions further. In natural labor, cervical stretch raises posterior pituitary oxytocin release, a positive feedback loop called the Ferguson reflex.
whyNot: A Gs-coupled rise in cyclic AMP relaxes uterine smooth muscle. This is how beta-2 agonists slow contractions.
Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated channels at skeletal neuromuscular junctions and autonomic ganglia, not oxytocin receptors on myometrium.
Correct.
Oxytocin is a peptide and acts on a surface G protein-coupled receptor. Nuclear receptors bind steroid and thyroid hormones.

questions.stem: On the second day after delivery, the mother has a temperature of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), lower abdominal pain, a tender uterus, and foul-smelling lochia. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness. Which of the following best explains her condition?
options: Ascending polymicrobial infection of the decidua
Chronic plasma cell infiltration of the endometrial stroma
Cyclic bleeding from ectopic endometrial tissue
Hematogenous seeding of the kidney by enteric bacteria
approach: Note the setting: fever and uterine tenderness soon after delivery, with prolonged rupture of membranes and fever in labor.
These point to acute endometritis, an infection of the decidua by organisms ascending from the lower genital tract.
Separate it from chronic endometritis, which is identified by plasma cells and causes milder, long-lasting symptoms.
questions.why: Acute postpartum endometritis is a polymicrobial infection of the decidua by vaginal and bowel flora, including group B streptococci, anaerobes, and gram-negative rods. Prolonged rupture of membranes, intra-amniotic infection, cesarean delivery, and retained products of conception raise the risk. It causes fever, uterine tenderness, and foul lochia within the first few days after delivery. Chronic endometritis is a different disorder, defined by plasma cells in the endometrial stroma.
whyNot: Correct.
Plasma cells in the endometrial stroma define chronic endometritis, which causes irregular bleeding or pelvic pain over months, not high fever 2 days after delivery.
Ectopic endometrial tissue is endometriosis, which causes cyclic pelvic pain and is suppressed during pregnancy.
Pyelonephritis would cause flank or costovertebral angle tenderness, and it usually ascends from the bladder.

questions.stem: The mother asks whether breastfeeding will give her baby antibodies to help clear the bloodstream infection. Which of the following best describes the main antibody in her breast milk?
options: IgD that binds the infant's naive B cells
IgM that is absorbed into the infant's blood
IgE that sensitizes the infant's mast cells
Secretory IgA that acts in the infant's gut
approach: Recall the two routes of passive immunity: placental IgG before birth and breast milk after birth.
The main antibody in milk is secretory IgA, a dimer protected from digestion by its secretory component.
It acts on the infant's mucosal surfaces and is not absorbed in useful amounts, so it does not treat bloodstream infection.
questions.why: Breast milk, especially colostrum, is rich in secretory IgA, which binds microbes and toxins in the infant's gut and respiratory tract and blocks their attachment. The secretory component protects it from digestive enzymes, but it stays in the lumen and does not reach the blood in useful amounts. Systemic protection in a newborn comes from maternal IgG moved across the placenta by FcRn before birth. Antibiotics are what treat this infant's sepsis.
whyNot: IgD is found mainly on the surface of naive B cells. It is not a meaningful antibody in milk.
IgM is present in milk only in small amounts, and it is not absorbed into the infant's blood.
IgE mediates allergic reactions and is not the main protective antibody in milk.
Correct.

case: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, comes to the physician at 12 weeks' gestation because of vaginal spotting for 4 days. Uterine size is consistent with dates. Serum beta-hCG is 92,000 mIU/mL. Ultrasonography shows a growth-restricted fetus and an enlarged placenta containing scattered cystic spaces. Karyotype of chorionic villi is 69,XXY. Tissue from suction evacuation shows a mixture of normal-sized villi and swollen villi with irregular outlines and focal trophoblast proliferation, and the villous cytotrophoblast stains positive for p57. Diagnosis: partial hydatidiform mole.

questions.stem: Which of the following events most likely produced the karyotype of this conceptus?
options: Fertilization of an ovum lacking its nucleus by one sperm that then duplicated
Retention of the second polar body after fertilization by one sperm
Fertilization of a normal haploid ovum by two sperm
Nondisjunction of chromosome 21 in maternal meiosis I
approach: Count chromosome sets: 69 chromosomes is triploid, one maternal set and two of another origin.
A molar placenta with excess trophoblast points to an extra paternal set, because paternal genes drive trophoblast growth.
The usual cause is two sperm fertilizing one normal ovum (dispermy).
questions.why: A partial mole is triploid with one maternal and two paternal sets, most often from dispermy. The extra paternal genome drives trophoblast overgrowth, while the maternal set allows some fetal development, so fetal parts are present. Because a maternal genome is present, maternally expressed p57 stains the cytotrophoblast. A complete mole is usually 46,XX with only paternal chromosomes from an empty ovum, has no fetal parts, shows diffuse villous swelling, and is p57 negative.
whyNot: An empty ovum fertilized by one sperm that duplicates gives a 46,XX complete mole with no maternal chromosomes, so p57 would be negative.
Retaining the second polar body adds an extra maternal set. That kind of triploidy usually gives a small placenta and no molar change.
Correct.
Nondisjunction of chromosome 21 gives trisomy 21 with 47 chromosomes, not a triploid set of 69.

questions.stem: In a normal pregnancy, the placenta makes large amounts of estriol, but it cannot build this hormone from cholesterol alone. Which of the following supplies the main precursor for placental estriol synthesis?
options: Maternal ovarian androstenedione
Corpus luteum progesterone
Maternal adrenal cortisol
Fetal adrenal DHEA sulfate
approach: Recall that the placenta lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase, so it cannot turn progesterone into androgens.
The fetal adrenal zone makes DHEA sulfate, which the fetal liver hydroxylates at the 16 position.
The placenta removes the sulfate and aromatizes the product to estriol.
questions.why: Estriol synthesis needs the fetus, the placenta, and the mother working together. The placenta lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase, so it depends on DHEA sulfate from the large fetal adrenal zone. The fetal liver converts it to 16-hydroxy-DHEA sulfate, and the placenta uses sulfatase and aromatase to make estriol. Separately, hCG keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over progesterone production near the end of the first trimester.
whyNot: Maternal ovarian androgens contribute little in pregnancy, and the 16-hydroxylation needed for estriol happens in the fetal liver.
The placenta can make progesterone, but without 17-alpha-hydroxylase it cannot convert progesterone to androgens or estrogens.
Cortisol is a glucocorticoid. The placenta inactivates much of it to cortisone, and it is not an estriol precursor.
Correct.

questions.stem: The hCG-secreting cells that cover the molar villi in this pregnancy descend from cells set aside before implantation. Which of the following parts of the blastocyst gave rise to these cells?
options: Epiblast
Trophoblast
Inner cell mass
Hypoblast
approach: Recall the blastocyst: an outer layer of trophoblast and an inner cell mass (embryoblast).
The trophoblast forms the cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast of the chorionic villi.
The inner cell mass splits into epiblast and hypoblast and forms the embryo.
questions.why: After cleavage, the morula forms a blastocyst with an outer cell layer called the trophoblast and an inner cell mass. The blastocyst implants at about day 6, when trophoblast becomes cytotrophoblast and invasive syncytiotrophoblast, which secretes hCG to maintain the corpus luteum. The cells covering the villi, including the overgrown cells in this mole, come from this trophoblast, while the villous core comes from extraembryonic mesoderm. The inner cell mass forms the epiblast and hypoblast, which give rise to the embryo and the yolk sac lining.
whyNot: The epiblast forms the three germ layers of the embryo and the extraembryonic mesoderm of the villous core, but not the trophoblast that covers the villi.
Correct.
The inner cell mass becomes the embryo proper through the epiblast and hypoblast.
The hypoblast forms the lining of the primary yolk sac and does not form villi.

questions.stem: After evacuation, her serum hCG plateaus for 3 weeks and then rises. Pelvic MRI shows hydropic villous tissue extending deep into the myometrium, and chest imaging is normal. Which of the following complications is this lesion most likely to cause?
options: Uterine perforation with hemoperitoneum
Hemorrhagic metastases to the brain
Bilateral hydronephrosis from ureteral invasion
Transformation to squamous cell carcinoma
approach: Interpret the hCG: a plateau or rise after evacuation means persistent gestational trophoblastic disease.
Hydropic villi invading the myometrium define an invasive mole.
Its main danger is local: deep invasion can perforate the uterus and cause severe bleeding.
questions.why: An invasive mole is a hydatidiform mole whose swollen villi grow into the myometrium and sometimes into its vessels. It keeps making hCG, so levels fail to fall after evacuation. Because it is locally invasive, it can perforate the uterine wall and cause intraperitoneal hemorrhage. It follows complete moles more often than partial moles, and it responds well to chemotherapy.
whyNot: Correct.
Hemorrhagic brain metastases are typical of choriocarcinoma, which has no villi and spreads widely through the blood. Invasive mole rarely reaches the brain.
Ureteral invasion with hydronephrosis is a feature of advanced cervical carcinoma, not invasive mole.
Gestational trophoblastic disease does not turn into squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous carcinoma of the genital tract is linked to high-risk HPV.

dx: Anencephaly with polyhydramnios in a pregnancy with maternal folate deficiency
case: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, comes to the physician at 20 weeks' gestation for a routine ultrasound examination. She learned she was pregnant at 10 weeks and began prenatal vitamins then. Her diet has been low in fresh vegetables. Ultrasonography shows absence of the cranial vault and cerebral hemispheres above the orbits and an amniotic fluid index of 30 cm (5 to 24). Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is markedly increased. Her hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL (11.0 or more in pregnancy), serum folate is 2.1 ng/mL (more than 4.0), and fasting plasma glucose is 82 mg/dL (less than 92 in pregnancy). Diagnosis: anencephaly with polyhydramnios in a pregnancy with maternal folate deficiency.

questions.stem: Besides its role in thymidylate synthesis, folate supports rapid cell division in the closing neural tube through another reaction. Which of the following reactions also depends on folate?
options: One-carbon transfer in purine ring synthesis
Hydroxylation of proline residues in procollagen
Transamination of amino acids to keto acids
Carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate
approach: Recall that tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon units.
Two of its main jobs are making thymidylate and supplying carbons 2 and 8 of the purine ring, through 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate.
Without enough folate, DNA synthesis slows in fast-dividing tissues such as the neural folds, which must close by about day 28.
questions.why: Tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon units at different oxidation levels. N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate supplies the methyl group for thymidylate, and 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate supplies two carbons of the purine ring. Both are needed to make DNA, so folate deficiency slows division of rapidly growing cells. The neural tube closes by about day 28 after conception, often before a woman knows she is pregnant, which is why folic acid is advised before conception.
whyNot: Correct.
Proline hydroxylation in collagen synthesis requires vitamin C, not folate.
Transamination requires pyridoxal phosphate from vitamin B6.
Pyruvate carboxylation requires biotin.

questions.stem: The tissue that failed to close in this fetus came from one of the germ layers of the embryo. Which of the following describes this layer and when it formed?
options: Endoderm, formed by folding of the embryo in week 4
Ectoderm, formed by gastrulation in week 3
Hypoblast, formed in the bilaminar disc in week 2
Mesoderm, formed in the bilaminar disc in week 2
approach: Identify the defect: anencephaly is failure of the cranial neural tube (anterior neuropore) to close.
The neural tube forms from the neural plate, which is ectoderm induced by the notochord.
The three germ layers, including definitive ectoderm, are established by gastrulation in week 3.
questions.why: In week 2 the embryo is a bilaminar disc of epiblast and hypoblast. In week 3, gastrulation through the primitive streak forms the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The notochord then induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube. The cranial end closes at about day 25 and the caudal end at about day 28. Weeks 3 to 8 are when organs form and when teratogens and deficiencies cause the most major malformations.
whyNot: Endoderm forms the gut lining and its glands. It is not the source of the neural tube, and it is established in week 3, not week 4.
Correct.
The hypoblast forms the yolk sac lining and is displaced during gastrulation. It does not form the neural tube.
Mesoderm is formed during gastrulation in week 3. The bilaminar disc of week 2 has no mesoderm.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the increased amniotic fluid volume in this pregnancy?
options: Fetal osmotic diuresis from maternal hyperglycemia
Reduced fetal urine output
Premature rupture of the fetal membranes
Impaired fetal swallowing of amniotic fluid
approach: Recall the balance of amniotic fluid: fetal urine adds fluid, and fetal swallowing removes it.
Anencephaly disrupts the brainstem control of swallowing, so fluid builds up.
Her normal fasting glucose rules out a diabetic cause.
questions.why: In the second half of pregnancy, amniotic fluid is made mainly by fetal urine and removed mainly by fetal swallowing. Polyhydramnios results when swallowing is impaired, as in anencephaly or esophageal atresia, or when urine output is high, as in maternal diabetes. Oligohydramnios results from low fetal urine output, as in bilateral renal agenesis or urinary obstruction, and can lead to Potter sequence.
whyNot: Maternal hyperglycemia can cause fetal osmotic diuresis and polyhydramnios, but her fasting glucose is normal.
Reduced fetal urine output causes oligohydramnios, the opposite finding.
Rupture of the membranes lets fluid leak out and lowers amniotic fluid volume.
Correct.

questions.stem: Additional studies show a mean corpuscular volume of 87 fL (80 to 100), red cell distribution width of 18.5% (11.5 to 14.5), and serum ferritin of 8 ng/mL (15 to 150). Which of the following best explains her normal mean corpuscular volume despite folate deficiency?
options: Normal red cell size in physiologic dilutional anemia
Coexisting vitamin B12 deficiency
Coexisting iron deficiency with small red cells
Hemolysis that releases large reticulocytes into the blood
approach: Interpret the labs: low ferritin means iron deficiency, and low folate means a cause of large cells.
Microcytic iron deficiency and macrocytic folate deficiency together can average out to a normal MCV.
A high RDW shows that the cells vary widely in size, which reveals the mixed picture.
questions.why: Iron needs rise sharply in pregnancy because the red cell mass expands and the fetus and placenta take up iron, so iron deficiency is common. Folate deficiency makes large red cells and iron deficiency makes small ones. When both are present, the average cell size can be normal while the RDW is high, because the blood holds a mix of small and large cells. A low ferritin confirms the iron deficiency. Physiologic dilutional anemia, by contrast, has a normal MCV, normal RDW, and normal ferritin.
whyNot: Dilutional anemia of pregnancy has a normal ferritin and normal RDW. Her ferritin is low and her RDW is high.
Vitamin B12 deficiency also makes large red cells, so it would raise the MCV further. It would not explain her low ferritin.
Correct.
Hemolysis would raise reticulocytes, bilirubin, and LDH, and ferritin would not be low.
